explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: Zedekiah, his officers and the people of the land "…refused to obey the words that the LORD had spoken through Jeremiah the prophet." (Jeremiah 37:2) Jeremiah, a prophet who speaks for the LORD, was handing them the words, and they weren't taking them. That's a whole lot of people all saying no to the same thing.

You've got it, friend. The text says Zedekiah, his officers and the people of the land "…refused to obey the words that the LORD had spoken through Jeremiah the prophet." (Jeremiah 37:2) The words came through Jeremiah, and the king, his officers and the people of the land refused to obey them. That's like hearing the oven timer and deciding it's a suggestion.

explanations.answer: Pray to the LORD our God for us
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Jehucal and Zephaniah bring the message, "Please pray to the LORD our God for us!" (Jeremiah 37:3) The king asks for prayer and still hasn't obeyed. I'd call that a strange order of things, and I'd also say the text just reports it and leaves it there.

explanations.answer: Give us a sign from the LORD our God
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, but the text doesn't say that. The king's message is, "Please pray to the LORD our God for us!" (Jeremiah 37:3) Nothing in the verse asks for a sign. That's like ordering chocolate chip and getting handed raisin. Both are cookies, but it's still not what you asked for.

explanations.answer: Offer a sacrifice to the LORD for us
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Jehucal and Zephaniah the priest carry a different message: "Please pray to the LORD our God for us!" (Jeremiah 37:3) A priest is among the messengers, so I see why a sacrifice came to mind. But the verse only has the king asking for prayer.

Yes, friend. The Chaldeans, who were besieging Jerusalem, heard the report and "…withdrew from Jerusalem." (Jeremiah 37:5) The army that had been besieging the city pulled back. I bet that gave the city a little room to breathe.
Not this one, friend. The text says the Chaldeans "…withdrew from Jerusalem." when they heard the report. (Jeremiah 37:5) They didn't break in, they pulled back. The city got a pause, not a break-in.

Good guess if you were picturing a siege, friend, but that's not what happens here. When the Chaldeans heard the report, they "…withdrew from Jerusalem." (Jeremiah 37:5) They had been besieging the city, and this time they pulled away from it.

explanations.answer: Go back to its own land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The LORD says Pharaoh's army, "…which has marched out to help you, will go back to its own land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 37:7) The army that marched out to help is going to go home. So Judah can't build its hopes on it.

explanations.answer: Drive the Chaldeans out for good
explanations.explanation: Sounds like the dream, friend, but that's not what the LORD says. He says Pharaoh's army "…will go back to its own land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 37:7) Then the Chaldeans return (Jeremiah 37:8), so nobody is driving them out for good.
Not quite, friend. The LORD says Pharaoh's army "…will go back to its own land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 37:7) No camping outside the gates is mentioned. The army that came to help is headed home.

Yes, friend. The LORD says that after Pharaoh's army goes back, "…the Chaldeans will return and fight against this city. They will capture it and burn it down." (Jeremiah 37:8) It's a hard word to hear. The city's break from the siege won't last.

Not this time, friend. The text says the Chaldeans "…will return and fight against this city. They will capture it and burn it down." (Jeremiah 37:8) So the statement is true. It's a heavy word, and the LORD says it plainly.

explanations.answer: Get up and burn the city down
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The LORD says that even if only wounded men remained in their tents, "…they would still get up and burn this city down." (Jeremiah 37:10) Wounded men still getting up to finish the job! That tells you how sure this word is.

explanations.answer: Pack up their tents and go home
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. The LORD says those wounded men "…would still get up and burn this city down." (Jeremiah 37:10) They don't go home. Even a beaten-up army, he says, still gets the job done.

explanations.answer: Send word to Babylon for help
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The verse never mentions sending for help. It says the wounded men "…would still get up and burn this city down." (Jeremiah 37:10) They don't need backup in this picture. That's how strong the LORD's word is.

explanations.answer: Claim his portion there among the people
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. Jeremiah started to leave Jerusalem "…to go to the land of Benjamin to claim his portion there among the people." (Jeremiah 37:12) That's the reason the text gives. It's a plain errand, and it's about to go sideways.

explanations.answer: Hide away from King Zedekiah's men
explanations.explanation: Not what the text says, friend. Jeremiah was going to the land of Benjamin "…to claim his portion there among the people." (Jeremiah 37:12) Hiding isn't mentioned. He's just heading out on his own business.

explanations.answer: Bring the LORD's word to the towns
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, since Jeremiah is a prophet, friend. But the verse gives a different reason: he went "…to claim his portion there among the people." (Jeremiah 37:12) I'd say the text keeps it simple, so we do too.

Yes, friend. Irijah seized Jeremiah and said, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans!" (Jeremiah 37:13) The Chaldeans were the army that had been besieging the city. So it was a serious thing to say about a man at the gate.

Not this one, friend. Irijah says, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans!" (Jeremiah 37:13) Egypt's army had come to help Judah, so the accusation here points the other way. The Chaldeans are the ones named.

Not in this story, friend. Irijah seized Jeremiah and said, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans!" (Jeremiah 37:13) The Philistines don't show up anywhere in this passage. The Chaldeans are the ones named.

That's right, friend. Jeremiah said it was a lie, but Irijah "…would not listen to him; instead, he arrested Jeremiah and took him to the officials." (Jeremiah 37:14) No listening at all. I think that must have stung.
Not quite, friend. The text says Irijah "…arrested Jeremiah and took him to the officials." (Jeremiah 37:14) Priests aren't part of this step. It's the officials who get him.
Close, but no, friend. Irijah "…arrested Jeremiah and took him to the officials." (Jeremiah 37:14) Elders aren't mentioned in this scene. The officials are the ones the text names.

Yes, friend. "The officials were angry with Jeremiah…" (Jeremiah 37:15) The text gives that feeling plainly. The very next thing it says is that they beat him and placed him in jail. I think this part of the story is a heavy one.
Not here, friend. The text says "The officials were angry with Jeremiah…" (Jeremiah 37:15) The feeling it gives is anger, not being pleased. What follows is that they beat him and placed him in jail.
Not quite, friend. The text says "The officials were angry with Jeremiah…" (Jeremiah 37:15) Patience would have been a nice change, but that's not what the officials bring. Anger is what they bring.

explanations.answer: Zedekiah will be handed to Babylon's king
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Jeremiah answers the king, "You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." (Jeremiah 37:17) After all that time in the dungeon, he still gives the word straight. I think that took real courage.

explanations.answer: The Chaldeans will go away for good
explanations.explanation: Not what Jeremiah says, friend. That's the very idea the LORD warned against: "Do not deceive yourselves by saying, ‘The Chaldeans will go away for good,’ for they will not!" (Jeremiah 37:9) To the king, Jeremiah says, "You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." (Jeremiah 37:17)

explanations.answer: Pharaoh's army will come to rescue him
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The LORD had already said Pharaoh's army "…will go back to its own land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 37:7) So Jeremiah's word to the king is, "You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." (Jeremiah 37:17) That word is about Babylon's king, not Pharaoh's army.

That's right, friend. Jeremiah asks, "How have I sinned against you or your servants or these people, that you have put me in prison?" (Jeremiah 37:18) He asks the king straight to his face. I think that's a man who knows he did nothing to earn this.

Not this time, friend. The statement is true. Jeremiah asks Zedekiah, "How have I sinned against you or your servants or these people, that you have put me in prison?" (Jeremiah 37:18) It's a bold question, and the text gives it just as it is.

explanations.answer: Babylon's king would not come against them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jeremiah asks, "Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, claiming, ‘The king of Babylon will not come against you or this land’?" (Jeremiah 37:19) Those prophets claimed Babylon's king would not come against them, and Jeremiah asks where they are now. That's a hard question to answer.

explanations.answer: Pharaoh's army would stay and fight for them
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The claim Jeremiah names is, "The king of Babylon will not come against you or this land…" (Jeremiah 37:19) Nothing about Pharaoh's army staying to fight. The prophets said Babylon wouldn't come at all.

explanations.answer: Egypt would rebuild the city's walls
explanations.explanation: Not in this passage, friend. Jeremiah quotes the prophets as claiming, "The king of Babylon will not come against you or this land…" (Jeremiah 37:19) Rebuilding walls never comes up. Their claim was that Babylon wouldn't come.

Not so, friend. Jeremiah had begged, "Do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, or I will die there." (Jeremiah 37:20) And the king "…gave orders for Jeremiah to be placed in the courtyard of the guard…" (Jeremiah 37:21) So Zedekiah did not send him back.

Right, friend. After Jeremiah's plea, "…King Zedekiah gave orders for Jeremiah to be placed in the courtyard of the guard…" (Jeremiah 37:21) He didn't send him back to Jonathan's house. Jeremiah's petition was heard.
Yes, friend! Jeremiah got "…a loaf of bread daily from the street of the bakers…" (Jeremiah 37:21) That's a street I'd like to visit. The bread kept coming until all the bread in the city was gone.

Not quite, friend. The loaf came "…from the street of the bakers…" (Jeremiah 37:21) I'd trust a potter with my mug, but when it's time for the loaf, the text sends us to the bakers. Jeremiah got one every day, until all the bread in the city was gone.

Close, but no, friend. The text says the daily loaf came "…from the street of the bakers…" (Jeremiah 37:21) A street of merchants might have had a little of everything, but this one is named for the people who work the dough. The loaf kept coming daily, until all the bread in the city was gone.
